title: Major Characteristics of the Manager's Job

segments.title: The Manager's Daily Pressures
segments.script: Picture the manager of a busy Shoprite branch in Soweto. Her day starts before the doors open and doesn't really end when they close, because problems follow her home on WhatsApp. This is the first truth about managing: time is always fragmented. You never get long, quiet stretches to think. You get five minutes here to solve a stock delivery issue, ten minutes there to calm down an angry customer, then a call from head office about targets. Researchers who studied managers found their work is short, broken into pieces, and mostly done through talking rather than writing. Working longer hours does not fix this, because a day only has twenty four hours, and eventually extra hours produce less and less benefit, what we call diminishing returns. Second truth, values compete. Think of a taxi association leader in Johannesburg. The drivers want more income per trip. Commuters want cheap, fast, safe rides. Owners of the taxis want the vehicles maintained and profits protected. The leader cannot make everyone happy at once. Decisions usually get made based on what is most urgent and what is closest to blowing up, not on some perfect formula. Third truth, the job has become overloaded. Many organisations, including South African firms, cut out layers of middle management to become leaner. That sounds efficient, but it meant the managers who remained suddenly had far more people reporting directly to them. Old management theory said seven direct reports was a sensible maximum. Now, thanks to cellphones, email, and instant messaging, some managers oversee twenty or thirty people directly. Because of all this, efficiency, doing more with the same or less time, has become the single most important skill a manager needs today. Two roles are also growing in importance. The entrepreneurial role means constantly scanning for threats and opportunities, like a spaza shop owner noticing a new competitor opening down the street, or spotting a gap to start selling airtime and electricity vouchers before anyone else does. The leadership role means being a mentor, not just a supervisor. If a skilled clinic nurse in a Joburg government clinic leaves, the whole department slows down until someone equally capable is trained, and even then, productivity dips for a while. Managers carry many responsibilities beyond just supervising, including long range planning, controlling resources, watching the wider business environment, coordinating between teams, handling customer and community relations, consulting internally on problems, and monitoring the quality of products and services. Not every manager does all of these equally. This depends heavily on where you sit in the organisation, whether you are an executive at the very top, a middle manager, or a first line manager working directly with frontline staff, and that hierarchy shapes exactly what your job looks like day to day.
keyPoints: Managerial time is fragmented, brief, and mostly verbal, not long blocks of quiet planning
Managers face competing demands from employees, customers, and shareholders and must prioritise by urgency
Downsizing increased the number of direct reports, making efficiency the core modern management skill
The entrepreneurial and leadership roles are growing because managers must spot opportunities and mentor talent
segments.altExplanation: Think of managing like being the only cashier during a taxi rank's busiest hour, with three queues forming at once, a delivery van blocking the entrance, and your phone ringing about a broken card machine. You cannot finish any one task properly before another interrupts you. That is fragmentation. Now imagine each queue wants something different, one wants speed, one wants a discount, one wants a receipt reprinted. You cannot satisfy all three fully, so you make a judgement call based on who is angriest or closest to leaving. That is competing values. And when the shop next door closes and sends its customers to you without hiring extra staff, that is overload, exactly what happened to many managers after organisations cut middle layers.
segments.deeper: The shift toward efficiency as the defining managerial skill reflects a broader change in how organisations are structured. Flatter hierarchies, driven by technology that allows instant communication and monitoring, mean fewer layers exist to absorb decision making and coordination. This places enormous pressure on remaining managers to triage constantly, deciding which fires to fight first. The growing importance of the entrepreneurial role connects to faster product cycles and quicker technological obsolescence, meaning managers cannot simply maintain existing operations, they must actively hunt for advantage. Similarly, the leadership role expands because talent has become a scarcer resource than capital or equipment in many industries. Losing a single highly capable employee can stall an entire unit, so managers must invest continuously in developing people rather than treating staffing as a one time hiring event. Together these forces mean the manager's job has moved away from routine caretaking toward active, constant judgement calls made with incomplete time and information, which is precisely why efficiency, prioritising correctly under pressure, has overtaken other skills as the defining mark of a capable modern manager.
segments.example: Consider an Eskom regional manager during a period of load shedding. Customers are furious about outages, technicians want more staff to fix ageing infrastructure faster, and head office wants costs controlled. The manager cannot fully satisfy all three. She prioritises repairing the substation serving a hospital first, because the risk there is most urgent and closest, even though a residential area has been complaining longer. This is competing values and time fragmentation playing out in a single afternoon of decisions.

checkpoint.prompt: Describe and explain the different levels of management.
checkpoint.answer: Management is the process of planning, organizing, directing, and controlling the activities of employees in combination with other resources to accomplish organizational goals. Managerial responsibilities include longrange planning, controlling, environmental scanning, supervision, coordination, customer relations, community relations, internal consulting, and monitoring of products and services. These responsibilities differ by level in the organizational hierarchy and by department or function. The twenty-first-century manager will differ from most current managers in four ways. In essence, he will be a global strategist, a master of technology, a good politician, and a premier leader-motivator.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must mention that management involves planning, organizing, directing, and controlling resources toward organisational goals, note that responsibilities differ by hierarchy level and by department or function, and reference the future manager needing to be a global strategist, technology master, skilled politician, and leader-motivator.

checkpoint.prompt: Why has efficiency become the core management skill in modern organisations, according to the passage?
options: Because managers have less time and more direct reports
checkpoint.answer: Because managers have less time and more direct reports

checkpoint.prompt: Explain in your own words what it means that a manager's values are in tension, using an example from your own life or community.
checkpoint.answer: It means a manager cannot fully satisfy employees, customers, and shareholders or owners at the same time, so decisions get made based on urgency and closeness of the problem rather than pleasing everyone.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must state that different stakeholder groups want conflicting things and that managers resolve this through urgency or proximity, not by satisfying everyone equally, and should include a plausible concrete example.

segments.title: Skills Across Levels and Departments
segments.script: Now let's talk about what skills a manager actually needs, and how that changes depending on where you sit and what department you work in. There are three broad types of managerial skill. Technical skills are the hands on knowledge of your specific field, like a bookkeeper at a small Durban manufacturing firm knowing exactly how to close the monthly accounts, or a production supervisor at a bottling plant knowing how the machinery actually works. Human relations skills are about working with people, understanding what motivates them, and managing group dynamics, like a stokvel treasurer who must keep twenty members feeling heard and fairly treated even when money is tight. Conceptual skills are the ability to see the whole picture, to understand how the finance department, the sales team, and the warehouse all fit together as one system, the kind of thinking a chief executive of a retail chain needs when deciding whether to open ten new stores across three provinces. These three skills are not equally important at every level. First line managers, the people directly supervising workers on the shop floor or in a call centre, rely heavily on technical skill because they need to understand the actual work being done and step in when something goes wrong. Middle managers sit in between, balancing all three skills fairly evenly, translating strategy from above into action below. Executive managers, the small team at the very top of the organisation, rely far more on conceptual skill and much less on technical skill, since their job is steering the whole ship rather than fixing individual machines. Human relations skill, though, matters at every single level, because whether you are supervising ten cashiers or leading a national company, you still need people to trust you and follow you. Beyond level, responsibilities also shift by department. A manufacturing manager focuses heavily on products, controlling quality, and supervising staff on the line. A marketing manager, by contrast, spends less time on internal coordination and planning and much more time on customer relationships and external contact, understanding what shoppers actually want. Accounting and human resources managers both do a lot of long range planning, but accounting concentrates on controlling budgets and tracking financial indicators, while human resources focuses on consulting, coordinating between departments, and managing relationships with unions or external training providers. Knowing this matters practically. If you are starting out, resist the urge to think and act like a chief executive before you have properly mastered being a first line supervisor, because the skills genuinely differ. And knowing which department emphasises which activities can help you choose a career path that matches your natural strengths, whether that is detailed technical work, people focused work, or big picture strategic thinking. Many companies rotate rising managers through different departments precisely so they build a well rounded set of skills before reaching the top.
keyPoints: Three managerial skills are technical, human relations, and conceptual, and their importance shifts by hierarchy level
First line managers need more technical skill, executives need more conceptual skill, human relations skill matters at every level
Responsibilities also differ by department, such as manufacturing focusing on products and control versus marketing focusing on customers
segments.altExplanation: Think of a game of soccer. The goalkeeper needs sharp technical skill, specific reflexes and positioning for one job. The team captain on the field needs strong people skills, reading teammates, motivating them mid match. The coach up in the stands needs conceptual skill, seeing the whole formation, how attack and defence connect, and adjusting strategy for the whole ninety minutes. Nobody expects the goalkeeper to coach from the goal line, and nobody expects the coach to make every save. Yet all three, keeper, captain, and coach, need to communicate and trust each other, which is like human relations skill running through every level of the team.
segments.deeper: The skill mix model helps explain common career frustrations. A talented technician promoted into first line management often struggles not because they lack ability, but because the job now demands more human relations skill than before, handling conflict, motivating a team, having difficult conversations, skills quite different from technical mastery. Similarly, a first line manager promoted straight to an executive role without middle management experience may struggle with conceptual work, seeing how departments interconnect, forecasting industry shifts, balancing competing strategic priorities across the whole organisation, because that muscle was never developed. This is partly why organisations rotate promising managers through multiple departments and levels rather than promoting purely on technical excellence. It also explains why departments differ so much in daily rhythm. A marketing manager's outward facing, relationship heavy work looks nothing like an accounting manager's controlling and monitoring focused work, even though both might report to the same executive team and both need long range planning skill. Recognising these differences helps individuals choose roles matching their strengths and helps organisations design more realistic promotion pathways rather than assuming any good employee can succeed at any managerial level immediately.
segments.example: Consider a young accountant promoted to branch manager at a bank in Polokwane. Her technical skill in finance was excellent, which is why she got promoted, but she suddenly needed strong human relations skill to manage twelve tellers with different personalities and grievances, and growing conceptual skill to understand how her branch's performance fit into the bank's regional strategy. Six months in, she realised the biggest challenge wasn't the numbers anymore, it was people and perspective, exactly the skill shift the model predicts as you move up.

checkpoint.prompt: Describe and explain the three types of managerial skills and how they relate to each level of management.
checkpoint.answer: Technical skills are the ability to use tools, procedures, and techniques of a specialised area, such as accounting principles or operations management. Human relations skills involve the ability to work with people and understand motivation and group processes. Conceptual skills involve organising and analysing information to see the organisation as a whole and understand how parts fit together. Executive positions require far more conceptual skill and less technical skill, first line managers require more technical skill and fewer conceptual skills, while human relations skills remain important at all three levels of the hierarchy.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must define all three skills, technical, human relations, and conceptual, and must state that executives need more conceptual and less technical skill, first line managers need more technical and less conceptual skill, and human relations skill is important at all levels.

checkpoint.prompt: Which level of management typically relies most on conceptual skills?
How does a marketing manager's focus typically differ from a manufacturing manager's focus, based on the passage?
checkpoint.answer: Marketing managers focus less on planning, coordinating, and internal consulting and more on customer relations and external contact, while manufacturing managers concentrate on products and services, controlling, and supervising staff.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must correctly contrast marketing's external customer focus against manufacturing's internal product, control, and supervision focus.
